title: Prehistoric Eastern Arabia
subtitle: c.8000–3000 BC · Green Arabia, the Arabian Neolithic and the World's First Pearl Fishers

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No kings — culture-horizons and the slow emergence of settled communities

entries.label: Marawah island — the earliest stone architecture in Arabia
entries.hint: Multi-room drystone houses on Marawah are the oldest built structures yet found in the UAE and among the oldest in the Arabian Peninsula. Their permanence marks a shift from mobile foraging to anchored coastal communities living off fish, shellfish and small herds.
entries.note: Excavations by Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism / TDIC, dir. Abdulla Al Kaabi and Mark Beech; radiocarbon dates c.5500–4700 BC. Beech, Cuttler et al., 'New evidence for the Neolithic settlement of Marawah', PSAS 35 (2005).

entries.label: Dalma island community — dates, pottery and Gulf-wide contact
entries.hint: A settled community on Dalma left plastered floors, Ubaid-type painted sherds carried from Mesopotamia, and charred date stones — some of the earliest evidence anywhere for people eating dates. The island shows how thoroughly the Neolithic Gulf was networked.
entries.note: Flavin & Shepherd 1994; Beech & Shepherd, 'Archaeobotanical evidence for early date consumption on Dalma Island, United Arab Emirates', Antiquity 75 (2001).

entries.label: Jebel al-Buhais — an inland herding society and its cemetery
entries.hint: At the desert-edge spring of al-Buhais, a community herding domestic sheep, goat and cattle buried its dead in a large collective cemetery over centuries. It is the fullest picture of an inland Arabian Neolithic society yet excavated.
entries.note: H.-P. and M. Uerpmann, S. Jasim et al., 'The Natural Environment of Jebel al-Buhais' and 'Funeral Monuments and Human Remains from Jebel al-Buhais' (2000–2008); AVA-Forschungen.

entries.label: As-Sabiyah — an Ubaid-linked settlement on Kuwait Bay
entries.hint: The H3 site on Kuwait Bay yielded Ubaid pottery, a painted ceramic boat model and bitumen slabs bearing barnacle and reed impressions — traces of reed boats caulked with Mesopotamian bitumen. It anchors the northern end of the Neolithic Gulf network.
entries.note: R. Carter & H. Crawford (eds.), 'Maritime Interactions in the Arabian Neolithic: Evidence from H3, As-Sabiyah' (2010); Carter, 'Boat remains and maritime trade in the Persian Gulf', Antiquity 80 (2006).

entries.label: The 'Dark Millennium' — settlement retreat c.4000–3200 BC
entries.hint: As the monsoon withdrew and the interior dried, dated sites across eastern Arabia thin out sharply for roughly eight centuries. Populations contracted onto the coast and a few springs; the record only recovers as the oasis-and-tomb landscape of the Bronze Age takes shape.
entries.note: P. Magee, 'The Archaeology of Prehistoric Arabia' (2014), ch. 4; Uerpmann 2003 on the 'Dark Millennium'; Preston & Parker on mid-Holocene aridification.

entries.label: Hafit horizon begins — cairn tombs and the first oasis villages
entries.hint: Beehive cairn tombs strung along the ridges of Jebel Hafit, and the earliest mud-brick at Hili and Bat, mark the resettlement of the interior at the very end of this folio's span. The Hafit period opens the Bronze Age story told in the Magan folio.
entries.note: Named from tombs at Jebel Hafit excavated by the Danish expedition (1959–62); K. Frifelt, 'The Island of Umm an-Nar' vol. 1. Dates c.3200–2700 BC bridge into the Magan folio.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Scarce and small-scale — what the skeletons and the arrowheads record

entries.label: Projectile injuries in the al-Buhais cemetery
entries.hint: A minority of the al-Buhais dead show healed or perimortem trauma, including flint arrow tips lodged in bone. The evidence points to occasional lethal violence between individuals or small groups, not organised warfare.
entries.note: Kiesewetter, Uerpmann & Jasim, 'Neolithic jewellery from Jebel al-Buhais 18', PSAS 30 (2000); Uerpmann et al., palaeopathology of the BHS-18 skeletal series.

entries.label: Contested access to springs and wells
entries.hint: As surface water failed during the arid hiatus, the few permanent springs and hand-dug wells became chokepoints. Clustered burials and repeated reoccupation of the same water sources suggest kin groups asserting durable claims over them.
entries.note: Inferential, following Magee 2014 and Charpentier's survey work on Holocene water sources in south-east Arabia; no fortification is attested this early.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Kinship, collective monuments and the management of shared water

entries.label: The collective cemetery as a claim on place
entries.hint: Hundreds of individuals of both sexes and all ages were buried together at al-Buhais over many generations, with grave goods distributed fairly evenly. A cemetery reused this long is itself an institution — it marked the group's territory and encoded its right to the spring.
entries.note: Uerpmann, Uerpmann & Jasim (eds.), 'The Archaeology of Jebel al-Buhais' vols. 1–3 (2000–2008); c.450 individuals recorded at BHS-18.

entries.label: Desert 'kites' — cooperative hunting architecture
entries.hint: Long low stone walls funnelling gazelle and oryx into killing enclosures required many hands to build and to work. These 'kites' are the clearest prehistoric evidence in Arabia of labour organised beyond the single household.
entries.note: D. Kennedy, 'Kites in Saudi Arabia', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy (2011); Aerial Photographic Archive for Archaeology in the Middle East (APAAME) survey of Arabian kites.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The sea in the grave — animals, ornament and the Akab dugong mound

entries.label: Ornament and animal offerings in Neolithic burials
entries.hint: Al-Buhais burials contain thousands of beads of shell, carnelian and mother-of-pearl, pierced pendants, and the bones of goats and gazelles placed with the dead. Consistent treatment across the cemetery implies a shared body of belief about death.
entries.note: Kiesewetter, Uerpmann & Jasim, 'Neolithic jewellery from Jebel al-Buhais 18', PSAS 30 (2000).

entries.label: The Akab dugong bone mound
entries.hint: On Akab, people stacked the skulls and bones of dozens of butchered dugongs into a deliberate mound, arranging skulls in rows and adding stone tools and beads. It is one of the earliest ritual monuments known from the Arabian coast, built around a sea mammal.
entries.note: S. Méry, V. Charpentier et al., 'A dugong bone mound: the Neolithic ritual site of Akab in Umm al-Quwain', Antiquity 83 (2009).

entries.label: Early rock art of the Hajar mountains
entries.hint: Pecked images of hunters, ibex, snakes and later camels cover rock faces across the Hajar range. The oldest panels — weathered hunting scenes beneath datable Bronze Age additions — likely reach back into this period, though rock art resists precise dating.
entries.note: M. Ziolkowski, 'The rock art of the UAE', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy (2007); relative dating by superimposition and patination only.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Beadwork, painted pottery and a clay model of a boat

entries.label: The al-Buhais bead industry
entries.hint: Buhais artisans ground and drilled beads from Gulf shell, imported carnelian and soft stone, producing standardised forms in enormous quantity. The skill and volume make bodily ornament the signature craft of the inland Neolithic.
entries.note: Kiesewetter, Uerpmann & Jasim, PSAS 30 (2000); microdrilling analysis in the BHS-18 small-finds reports.

entries.label: Ubaid painted pottery on the Arabian shore
entries.loc: Gulf coast: As-Sabiyah, Dalma, Marawah, Bahrain (al-Markh)
entries.hint: Fine buff pottery painted with geometric bands in dark pigment — made in southern Mesopotamia — turns up at Neolithic sites the length of the Arabian coast. Local communities had no pottery of their own; these vessels were prestige imports.
entries.note: R. Carter, 'The chronology and distribution of Ubaid pottery in the Gulf', in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

entries.label: The As-Sabiyah ceramic boat model
entries.hint: A small painted clay model of a high-prowed reed boat, found with bitumen boat fragments, is among the oldest representations of a watercraft anywhere. It shows that the people using the Gulf as a highway also depicted the vessels that carried them.
entries.note: R. Carter, 'Boat remains and maritime trade in the Persian Gulf', Antiquity 80 (2006); Carter & Crawford (eds.), H3 As-Sabiyah final report (2010).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Knowledge without writing — tides, stars and the sourcing of stone

entries.label: Tidal and seasonal timing encoded in coastal sites
entries.hint: Fish-trap alignments, the seasonality of pearl-oyster and fish remains, and the scheduling of island occupation show communities working to a detailed calendar of tides, winds and fish runs — practical astronomy and marine ecology carried entirely in memory.
entries.note: M. Beech, 'In the Land of the Ichthyophagi' (2004), on Gulf fishing seasonality; Charpentier on tidal fish-trap systems of south-east Arabia.

entries.label: Selective procurement of flint and carnelian
entries.hint: Neolithic knappers travelled to specific outcrops for the best flint and returned repeatedly to the same carnelian sources, bypassing nearer but poorer stone. The pattern implies a shared, transmitted map of where good raw material could be found.
entries.note: Uerpmann, lithic raw-material sourcing in the Buhais region reports; Charpentier, Charpentier 2008 on Holocene foragers of the interior (2008).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Herding, fishing and the beginning of the pearl fishery — the Gulf's oldest livelihood

entries.label: The Neolithic herding package reaches Arabia
entries.hint: Domestic sheep, goat and cattle — none of them native to Arabia — appear together at inland sites in the sixth millennium BC, brought across from the Levant or via Mesopotamia. Herding, alongside hunting, became the basis of interior life.
entries.note: H.-P. Uerpmann & M. Uerpmann, faunal analyses from Jebel al-Buhais and Jebel Faya; Drechsler, 'The Dispersal of the Neolithic over the Arabian Peninsula' (2009).

entries.label: The world's oldest pearl — Marawah, c.5800 BC
entries.hint: A natural pearl recovered from a Neolithic house floor on Marawah is the oldest known anywhere. Pearl-oyster shell at Marawah, Dalma and Umm al-Quwain shows Gulf communities were already diving for and valuing pearls eight thousand years ago — the start of a trade that defined the region until the 1930s.
entries.note: Announced 2019 by Abu Dhabi Department of Culture and Tourism ('Abu Dhabi Pearl'); context published by Beech et al. in the Marawah MR-11 excavation reports.

entries.label: Neolithic fishing and shellfish economies
entries.hint: Coastal middens metres deep in fish bone and shell, barbed hooks of pearl shell, and net weights show intensive, near-industrial exploitation of the sea. Tuna and jack were caught offshore; dugong and turtle were taken in the shallows.
entries.note: V. Charpentier, Charpentier, PSAS 38 (2008), PSAS 38 (2008); Ra's al-Hamra RH-5 fish-bone studies, Salvatori & Uerpmann.

entries.label: Early date-palm use on Dalma
entries.hint: Charred date stones from Dalma are among the earliest evidence for date consumption anywhere. Whether the palms were tended or wild is unclear, but the date — storable, sugar-rich, salt-tolerant — was already part of the Gulf diet before farming villages existed.
entries.note: Beech & Shepherd, 'Archaeobotanical evidence for early date consumption on Dalma Island', Antiquity 75 (2001).

entries.label: Aridification forces a coastal economy
entries.hint: When the monsoon rains withdrew, interior herding collapsed and surviving communities concentrated on the coast, living on fish, shellfish and mangrove resources. The Gulf littoral became a refuge — a pattern repeated in every later Arabian drought.
entries.note: Parker et al., 'A record of Holocene climate change from lake geochemical analyses in south-eastern Arabia', Quaternary Research (2006); Magee 2014, ch. 4.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Reed boats, bitumen caulking, drystone building and the pressure-flaked point

entries.label: Reed boats caulked with bitumen
entries.hint: Slabs of bitumen from As-Sabiyah preserve the impressions of reed bundles on one face and barnacles on the other — the coated hulls of seagoing reed boats. Mesopotamian bitumen made Gulf-wide voyaging possible a full millennium before the sail is attested.
entries.note: R. Carter, Antiquity 80 (2006); bitumen sourcing to Mesopotamian seeps by Connan et al.

entries.label: Drystone architecture at Marawah
entries.hint: The Marawah houses — coursed beachrock walls forming several connected rooms, with plastered surfaces — are the earliest substantial masonry in south-east Arabia and a template for the stone-built settlements of the Bronze Age.
entries.note: Beech, Cuttler et al., PSAS 35 (2005); DCT Abu Dhabi Marawah reports.

entries.label: The Arabian bifacial point tradition
entries.hint: Neolithic Arabian knappers produced finely pressure-flaked, tanged and barbed arrowheads — the 'Fasad' and later types — the peninsula's most distinctive lithic technology and a marker used to trace Neolithic populations across the interior.
entries.note: J. Rose & V. Usik, 'The Upper Palaeolithic of South Arabia'; Charpentier's typology of south-east Arabian points.

entries.label: Standardised bead-drilling
entries.hint: Consistent perforation diameters across thousands of Buhais beads imply a shared drilling technique using stone or possibly copper-tipped bow drills — a repeatable, teachable craft process rather than ad hoc production.
entries.note: Kiesewetter, Uerpmann & Jasim, PSAS 30 (2000); use-wear on BHS-18 drill points.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Gulf's first long-distance network — Mesopotamia to the Arabian shore and back

entries.label: The Ubaid maritime network, Kuwait to Qatar to the UAE
entries.hint: For a thousand years, southern Mesopotamian communities sent pottery, bitumen and beads down the Arabian coast by boat, receiving pearls, shell and possibly dried fish in return. It is the earliest sustained long-distance exchange system documented anywhere in the region.
entries.note: R. Carter, 'The Ubaid and the Gulf', in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010); Oates, Davidson, Kamilli & McKerrell, 'Seafaring merchants of Ur?', Antiquity 51 (1977).

entries.label: Herding, pottery use and boat-building spread south
entries.hint: Domestic animals, the habit of using fine painted pottery, and bitumen boat technology all entered eastern Arabia from the north within the same window. The Neolithic Gulf was a receiving zone plugged into the wider Near Eastern world.
entries.note: Drechsler, 'The Dispersal of the Neolithic over the Arabian Peninsula' (2009); Uerpmann on the Levantine origin of the south-east Arabian herding package.

entries.label: Gulf shell and pearl reach Mesopotamia
entries.hint: Mother-of-pearl inlay and marine shell in the earliest levels of southern Mesopotamian towns come from the Gulf. The exchange ran both ways: the resources that made the Gulf worth visiting were already moving north before the first cities.
entries.note: Reese, 'Marine shells in the Levant and Mesopotamia'; Ubaid-period shell from Eridu and Ur reported by Oates et al. (1977).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Green Arabia, the flooding of the Gulf basin and the end of the humid phase

entries.label: Modern humans through Arabia — Jebel Faya, c.125,000 BP
entries.hint: Stone tools from the base of the Jebel Faya rock-shelter, dated by luminescence to about 125,000 years ago, resemble East African toolkits and predate the classic 'northern route' out of Africa. They put anatomically modern humans in south-east Arabia far earlier than expected — the deep prehistory beneath everything else in this folio.
entries.note: S. Armitage, S. Jasim, A. Marks, A. Parker et al., 'The Southern Route Out of Africa: Evidence for an Early Expansion of Modern Humans into Arabia', Science 331 (2011).

entries.label: The Holocene Humid Period — 'Green Arabia'
entries.hint: A northward shift of the monsoon filled the interior with lakes, grassland and savanna fauna — hippo, wild cattle, ostrich. This green window is what let herders and hunters spread across a peninsula that is now among the driest places on Earth.
entries.note: A. Parker & J. Rose, 'Climate change and human origins in southern Arabia', PSAS 38 (2008); lake records from Mundafan and Awafi.

entries.label: The Gulf basin floods to its modern shoreline
entries.hint: At the last glacial maximum the Gulf was largely dry, a river valley running to a shrunken sea near Hormuz. Post-glacial sea-level rise drowned it, reaching roughly today's coast by about 4000 BC and pushing coastal populations inland — the 'Gulf Oasis' scenario for early Arabian settlement.
entries.note: J. Rose, 'New Light on Human Prehistory in the Arabo-Persian Gulf Oasis', Current Anthropology 51 (2010); Lambeck, 'Shoreline reconstructions for the Persian Gulf since the last glacial maximum', EPSL (1996).

entries.label: The end of the humid phase and the mid-Holocene crisis
entries.hint: Around 4000 BC the monsoon retreated south, lakes dried and the interior became desert within a few centuries. The resulting settlement collapse — the 'Dark Millennium' — resets Arabian prehistory; what emerges afterward is the oasis-farming, tomb-building world of Dilmun and Magan.
entries.note: Parker et al., Quaternary Research (2006); Preston, Parker et al. on the 5.2–4.0 ka aridification of south-east Arabia.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Who the Neolithic dead were — gendered labour and equal graves

entries.label: Egalitarian burial at Jebel al-Buhais
entries.hint: Men, women, the elderly and infants at al-Buhais received broadly similar graves and grave goods, with no cluster of unusually rich burials. The cemetery records a society without marked hereditary rank — a baseline against which the hierarchical Bronze Age stands out.
entries.note: Uerpmann, Uerpmann & Jasim (eds.), BHS-18 mortuary analysis; grave-good distribution studies in 'The Archaeology of Jebel al-Buhais' vol. 2.

entries.label: Women's fishing toolkits at Ra's al-Hamra
entries.hint: At the RH-5 cemetery in Muscat, adult women were frequently buried with pearl-shell fish-hooks and net gear, men less consistently so. The pattern suggests women did much of the inshore fishing and shell-working that fed these communities.
entries.note: S. Salvatori, 'Death and ritual in a population of coastal food foragers: the Ra's al-Hamra 5 cemetery' (2007); Coppa et al., RH-5 bioarchaeology.

entries.label: A cared-for individual in the Buhais population
entries.hint: Several al-Buhais skeletons show healed serious fractures and degenerative disease that would have limited mobility for years, yet these people survived to be buried with the rest. Their survival depended on the group absorbing the cost of their care.
entries.note: Palaeopathology in the BHS-18 human-remains volume (Uerpmann et al.); healed long-bone fractures and advanced osteoarthritis recorded in the adult series.
